title: The Motivation and Zeal of Gospel Proclamation
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: Context of Apostolic Defense
subpoints: Criticism from 'super apostles' regarding Paul's rhetoric and demeanor
Paul's defense is motivated by protecting the integrity of the gospel
The passage is identified as a concise declaration of Christ's work

outline.title: Motivation: The Fear of the Lord
subpoints: Reverence and awe of God drive the desire to please Him
Awareness of the judgment seat of Christ compels evangelism
The goal is for others to face judgment in Christ, not on their own merits

outline.title: Motivation: The Love of Christ
subpoints: Christ's death for all signifies the death of the old self
Believers live no longer for themselves but for Him who rose again
This love compels the believer to persuade others of the truth

outline.title: Zeal in the Face of Accusation
subpoints: Paul accepts being called 'beside himself' if it means staying faithful to Scripture
Rejection of worldly wisdom in favor of biblical argumentation
Conscience is clear before God, validating the method of proclamation

summary:
In this morning service, Pastor Tito Lyro continues the sermon series on the second letter to the Corinthians, focusing on verses 11 through 13 of chapter 5. The message addresses the context of Paul’s defense against the 'super apostles' who criticized his rhetorical style and perceived fanaticism. It is emphasized that Paul’s self-defense is not for personal glory but to protect the credibility of the gospel message he preaches. The passage is highlighted by commentators as a profound and concise declaration of the work of Christ.

The sermon explores the dual motivations for gospel proclamation: the fear of the Lord and the love of Christ. The fear of the Lord is described as a reverential awe that drives believers to live pleasingly to God and to urge others to face the judgment seat of Christ in Christ rather than on their own merits. This is coupled with the compelling love of Christ, which transforms the believer’s identity from living for self to living for the One who died and rose again.

Finally, the message addresses the zeal required for this ministry. Paul’s willingness to be viewed as 'beside himself' or unsophisticated by worldly standards is presented as a testament to his commitment to biblical truth over rhetorical elegance. The clear conscience before God validates this approach, encouraging believers to remain steadfast in proclaiming the gospel despite external criticism.
